nodes.statement: Let h,qin mathbb Z with q square-free and gcd(h,q)=1. Let X,eta > 0 and suppose that -X/2leq h leq X^1+eta. Let G:mathbb Rtomathbb C be a smooth function supported on [1,2] that satisfies G^(j) ll_j X^j eta for all j geq 0. Let t:mathbb Z/qmathbb Z to mathbb C be a function. nodes.statement: The proof of the more general Theorem is a bit more involved. One has to first decompose t(n) into functions t^flat(n;q_0),q_0|q, which are balanced in the sense that they have mean value 0 over any coset of a non-trivial subgroup of mathbb Z/q_0mathbb Z. Applying the method separately for each t^flat(n;q_0) essentially gives us that K ll q \|t\|_2^2. Without this decomposition we would only be able to get K ll q \|t\|_1^2, potentially losing a factor of q for general t(n). The key property that is leveraged here is that the weight alpha(smqty(a & b \\ c &d)) = t(ad) is constant along certain one dimensional linear fibers in the two dimensional space Gamma_2(q,q) backslash SL_2(mathbb Z).
nodes.raw_latex: The proof of the more general Theorem \ref{thm:divisorperiodic} is a  bit more involved. One has to first decompose $t(n)$ into functions $t^{\flat}(n;q_0),q_0|q$, which are \emph{balanced} in the sense that they have mean value 0 over any coset of a non-trivial subgroup of ${\mathbb Z}/q_0{\mathbb Z}$. Applying the method separately for each $t^{\flat}(n;q_0)$ essentially gives us that $\mathcal{K} \ll q \|t\|_2^2$. Without this decomposition we would only be able to get $\mathcal{K} \ll q \|t\|_1^2$,  potentially losing a factor of $q$ for general $t(n)$. The key property that is leveraged here is that the weight $\alpha(\smqty(a & b \\ c &d)) = t(ad)$ is constant along certain one dimensional linear fibers in the two dimensional space $\Gamma_2(q,q) \backslash \operatorname{SL}_2({\mathbb Z})$.

By Proposition \ref{prop:specdecompL2} applied to $\tau_1$ we have
\begin{align}\nonumber
  K^{(\ell)}(\tau_1,\tau_2) = &  \frac{\mathbf{1}_{\chi \,\mathrm{principal}}}{|\Gamma \backslash G|} \langle K^{(\ell)}(\cdot,\tau_2) ,1 \rangle_{\Gamma \backslash G} + \sum_{\substack{V\in \mathcal{B}(q,\chi)\\ j \equiv \kappa \pmod{2}}}  \langle    K^{(\ell)}(\cdot,\tau_2), \varphi_V^{(j)} \rangle  \varphi_V^{(j)}(\tau_1)   \\
 \label{eq:prop71proof1} &+\sum_{\mathfrak{c}\in \mathfrak{C}(q,\chi)} \sum_{j \equiv \kappa \pmod{2}} \frac{1}{4 \pi i} \int_{(0)} \langle  K^{(\ell)}(\cdot,\tau_2), E^{(j)}_{\mathfrak{c}}(\cdot,\nu) \rangle E^{(j)}_{\mathfrak{c}}(g,\nu) \mathrm d \nu.
\end{align}
By unfolding the first term matches the first term in Proposition \ref{prop:boundbykernel}. We use unfolding to compute
\begin{align*}
    \langle    K^{(\ell)}(\cdot,\tau_2), \varphi_V^{(j)} \rangle =& \int_{\Gamma \backslash G}  K^{(\ell)}(g,\tau_2) \overline{\varphi_V^{(j)}(g)} \mathrm d g = \sum_{\gamma \in \Gamma} \int_{\Gamma \backslash G} \overline{\chi}(\gamma) k_{\ell,\ell}(\tau_2^{-1} \gamma g) \overline{\varphi_V^{(j)}(g)} \mathrm d g \\
=& \sum_{\gamma \in \Gamma} \int_{\gamma (\Gamma \backslash G)}  k_{\ell,\ell}(\tau_2^{-1}  g) \overline{\varphi_V^{(j)}(g)} \mathrm d g =\int_{ G}  k_{\ell,\ell}(\tau_2^{-1}g) \overline{\varphi_V^{(j)}(g)} \mathrm d g.
\end{align*}
With the Haar measure decomposition $\mathrm d g=  \mathrm d \mathrm{a} \mathrm d\mathrm{n}\mathrm d\mathrm{k}$ we get
\begin{align*}
    \int_{ G}  k_{\ell,\ell}(\tau_2^{-1}g) \overline{\varphi_V^{(j)}(g)} \mathrm d g = &\int_{\mathrm{N}} \int_{\mathrm{A}} \int_{\mathrm{K}} k_{\ell,\ell}(\tau_2^{-1}\mathrm{a}\mathrm{n} \mathrm{k}) \overline{\varphi_V^{(j)}( \mathrm{a}\mathrm{n} \mathrm{k})}  \mathrm d \mathrm{k} \mathrm d \mathrm{a} \mathrm d \mathrm{n} \\
    =&\int_{\mathrm{N}} \int_{\mathrm{A}} k_{\ell,\ell}( \tau_2^{-1}\mathrm{a}\mathrm{n} ) \overline{\varphi_V^{(j)}(\mathrm{a} \mathrm{n} )} \int_{\mathrm{K}} e^{i(\ell - j )\theta(\mathrm{k})} \mathrm d \mathrm{k} \mathrm d \mathrm{a} \mathrm d \mathrm{n}.
\end{align*}
The innermost integral is $1_{\ell=j}$. We recall that the $\varphi_V^{(l)}$ are eigenfunctions by \eqref{eq:varphieigenfuncOmega} and apply Proposition \ref{prop:integraloperator} to get
\begin{align} \nonumber
   \langle    K^{(\ell)}(\cdot,\tau_2), \varphi_V^{(\ell)} \rangle &=  \int_{ G}  k_{\ell,\ell}(\tau_2^{-1}g) \overline{\varphi_V^{(\ell)}(g)} \mathrm d g \\
  \nonumber &=L_{\ell,\ell} \overline{\varphi_V^{(\ell)} (\tau_2)}\\
\label{eq:prop71proof2}   &= \Phi_{\ell,\ell}(k;\nu_V) \overline{ \varphi_{V}^{(\ell)}(\tau_2)}.
\end{align}
Similar computation holds for the Eisenstein series contribution. Combining \eqref{eq:prop71proof1} and \eqref{eq:prop71proof2} Proposition \ref{prop:spectralexpofkernel} follows.

nodes.statement: Recall that H_ell(g)=e^iell (varphi+vartheta) and that, just as as in , we have for any U_lambda,ell of type (ell,ell) for some P_lambda,ell that U_lambda,ell(g)=H_ell(g)P_lambda,ell(u(g)). By Lemma we see that Omega U_lambda,ell=lambda U_lambda,ell is equivalent to (u(u+1) partial_u^2 + (2u+1) partial_u + lambda +fracell^24(u+1)) P_lambda,ell(u) = 0. Multiplying this with u/(u+1) (since u > 0) we get (u^2 partial_u^2 + ufrac(2u+1)u+1partial_u +fracu lambdau+1 +fracu ell^24(u+1)^2) P_lambda,ell(u)=0. Following the notation in ), this second order differential equation is of the form bigg( (z-c)^2 partial_z + (z-c) P(z) partial_z + Q(z)bigg) U(z) = 0 where c=0, P(z) = frac2z+1z+1, Q(z) =fracz lambdaz+1 +fracz ell^24(z+1)^2 . We then consider the indicial equation alpha^2+(p_0-1)alpha+q_0=0 with p_0&=P(0)=1\\ q_0&=Q(0)=0. In this case, the indicial equation has only the solution alpha=0 and as such there exist one solution for the differential equation which is analytic at u=0 and one with a logarithmic singularity . By U_lambda,ell(I)=1 and the fact that for g=I we have u=0, the function U_lambda,ell is uniquely determined to originate from the analytic solution. The claim is then clear since the integrals on the right-hand side define a type (ell,ell) eigenfunction with eigenvalue lambda.

Defining u(r;p) := 1_r equiv 0 pmodp - p^-1, u(r;q_0) := prod_p|q_0u(r;p), we have for square-free q 1_n equiv r pmodp = prod_p|q 1_n equiv r pmodp = prod_p|q (u(n-r;p) + p^-1) = sum_q_0 | q frac1q/q_0 u(n-r;q_0). Therefore, t(n) &= sum_r pmodq t(r) 1_n equiv r pmodp = sum_q_0 | q frac1q/q_0 sum_r pmodq t(r) u(n-r;q_0) \\ & = sum_q_0 | q t^flat(n;q_0), \\ t^flat(n;q_0) &:= sum_r_0 pmodq_0 t(r_0;q_0) u(n-r_0;q_0), \\ t(r_0;q_0) &:= frac1q/q_0sum_substackr pmodq \\ r equiv r_0 pmodq_0 t(r). Denote alpha(smqty(a & b \mathfrak c & d);q_0) := t^flat(ad;q_0). The parts where some p|q_0 divides one of a,b,c,d also need to be separated. To this end, we write for ad-bc=-h with gcd(h,q)=1 nonumber alpha(smqty(a & b \mathfrak c & d);q_0) &= alpha(smqty(a & b \mathfrak c & d);q_0) prod_p|q_0 bigg( 1_p|a+1_p|b + 1_substackp|c + 1_substackp |d -1_p|gcd(a,d) -1_p|gcd(b,c)+ 1_ gcd(abcd,p)=1 bigg) \\ &= sum_q_0=q_1 q_2 q_3q_4q_5 q_6 q_7 alpha(smqty(a & b \mathfrak c & d);q_0) prod_i=1^7 v_i(smqty(a & b \mathfrak c & d);q_i)=: sum_q_0=q_1 q_2 q_3q_4q_5 q_6 q_7 alpha(smqty(a & b \mathfrak c & d);q), where v_1(smqty(a & b \mathfrak c & d);q_1) = 1_q_1|a, v_2(smqty(a & b \mathfrak c & d);q_2) = 1_q_2|b, v_3(smqty(a & b \mathfrak c & d);q_3) = 1_q_3|c, v_4(smqty(a & b \mathfrak c & d);q_4) = 1_q_4|d, \\ v_5(smqty(a & b \mathfrak c & d);q_1) = 1_q_5|gcd(a,d), v_1(smqty(a & b \mathfrak c & d);q_1) = 1_q_6|gcd(b,c), v_1(smqty(a & b \mathfrak c & d);q_1) = 1_gcd(abcd,q_7)=1. Inserting this thrice and making a change of variables we have sum_ substackad-bc=-h G(ad/X) alpha(smqty(a & b \mathfrak c & d);q)&=int_mathbb R^3 sum_substackad-bc=-h G(ad/X)psi(a/A)psi(c/C)psi(d/D)alpha(smqty(a & b \mathfrak c & d);q) fracmathrm d A mathrm d C mathrm d DACD \\ &=: int_substack A D leq 2 X \\ C leq 2(X+|h|) S_psi(A,C,D) fracmathrm d A mathrm d C mathrm d DACD. Denote also B := (X+h)/C. By symmetry (ad leftrightarrow bc, a leftrightarrow d, b leftrightarrow c) we may assume that C ll X^eta D ll X^eta A ll X^2eta B. Note that here we have used the assumption -X/2leq h leq X^1+eta to infer that X ll AD ll BC ll X^1+eta . Recall Q_1,Q_2 from . If A > X^2eta Q_1 C or D > X^2eta Q_2 C, we obtain the right main term with sufficiently small error term by Poisson summation. For example, for A > X^2eta Q_1 C we have &sum_substackad-bc=-h G(ad/X)psi(a/A)psi(c/C)psi(d/D) alpha(smqty(a & b \mathfrak c & d);q) \\ & = sum_substacka,c,d \ad equiv -h pmod c G(ad/X)psi(a/A)psi(c/C)psi(d/D) alpha(smqty(a & b \mathfrak c & d);q) where a has a smooth weight on a asymp A. Splitting into residue classes pmod Q_1 and pmodc, combining the two residue classes, applying Poisson summation on a (using A geq X^2eta Q_1 C), we get the expected main term and an error term ll_J X^-J for any J>0. It remains to consider the complementary range of , where we can assume that X^-etall fracAC leq Q_1 X^2eta, X^-eta ll fracDC leq Q_2 X^2eta . We now apply Theorem to S_psi(A,C,D) with Gamma &= Gamma_2(Q_1,Q_2)\\ beta_h_0&=1_h_0=-h, gamma_k=1_k=1, xi_h=1, \\ alpha(smqty(a& b \\ c & d)) &= alpha(smqty(a & b \mathfrak c & d);q) = alphabigg(mqty(afrac-had-bc & bfrac-had-bc \mathfrak c & d);qbigg) in A(Q_1,Q_2,1,1), where the last expression for alpha extends its definition to M_2(mathbb Z) with determinant coprime to q. As we are only interested in k=1, we can adopt the notation in Remark and we have by Lemma |w(smqty( pm 1 & b \\ & pm 1))|&ll_varepsilon q^varepsilon (b,q_7) N(t). Thus, since X^-eta ll D/C leq Q_2 X^2eta, we have with K_+ = Q_2 N_h(t). Note that this matches the contribution from b=0 for q_7=q_0, which is the generic case. We also have by X^-eta leq A/C leq Q_1 X^2eta, C,D ll X^1/2+O(eta) R_1&leq X^O(eta) h^vartheta_qleft(1+bigg(fracXh Q_2 bigg)^theta right)left(1+ bigg(frac1 Q_2bigg)^1/2-thetaright)leq X^O(eta) h^thetaleft(1+bigg(fracXh Q_2 bigg)^theta right), \\ R_2&leq X^O(eta) left(1+bigg(frac X Q_2bigg)^theta right)left(1+ bigg(frach Q_2 bigg)^1/2-thetaright), and R_0 = X^O(eta) frac \|beta\|_1 A^1/2 \|beta\|_2 Q_1^1/2 C^1/2leq X^O(eta) . Therefore, by Theorem the error term is for h leq Q_2, using R_2, ll X^1/2+theta+O(eta) q_0^1/2-thetaN_h(t)^1/2 and for h geq Q_2, using R_1, ll X^1/2 +O(eta) q_0^1/2 N_h(t)^1/2 h^theta + X^1/2+theta +O(eta) q_0^1/2-theta N_h(t)^1/2. Thus, in either case we get ll X^1/2+O(eta) q_0^1/2N_h(t)^1/2 h^theta + X^1/2+theta+O(eta) q_0^1/2-thetaN_h(t)^1/2. The main term may be computed by reversing the smooth dyadic partition and reversing the decomposition .

nodes.statement: We require another decomposition of t(n). To this end, define u_0(n;q_0) &:= 1_n equiv 0 pmodq_0, u_h(n;q_1): = 1_n equiv -h pmodq_1, \\ v(n;p) &:= 1_n not equiv 0,-h pmodp, v(n;q_2) = prod_p|q_2 v(n;p). Then t(n) = t(n) prod_p|q bigg(u_0(n;p) + u_h(n;p) + v(n;p) bigg) = sum_q=q_0 q_1 q_2 t(n) u_0(n;q_0) u_h(n;q_1) v(n;q_2). This gives a decomposition of t(n) into d_3(q)ll_varepsilon q^varepsilon functions t(n) u_0(n;q_0) u_h(n;q_1) v(n;q_2). Then Theorem follows by applying Proposition separately for each of these, since N_h &bigg(t(n) u_0(n;q_0) u_h(n;q_1) v(n;q_2)bigg) \\ & = sum_r_1,r_2 pmodq |t(r_1) t(r_2)| prod_p_0|q_0 u_0(r_1;p_0) u_0(r_2;p_0) U_h(r_1,r_2;p_0) \\ & hspace110pt times prod_p_1|q_1 u_h(r_1;p_1) u_h(r_2;p_1) U_h(r_1,r_2;p_1) \\ & hspace110pt times prod_p_2|q_2 v(r_1;p_2) v(r_2;p_2) U_h(r_1,r_2;p_2) \\ & ll sum_r_1,r_2 pmodq |t(r_1) t(r_2)| prod_p|q bigg( 1_r_1 equiv r_2 pmodp + p^-1 bigg) \\ & ll sum_q=q_1 q_2 frac1q_2 sum_substackr_1,r_2 pmodq \\ r_1 equiv r_2 pmodq_1 |t(r_1) t(r_2)| \\ & ll sum_q=q_1 q_2 frac1q_2 sum_substackr_1,r_2 pmodq \\ r_1 equiv r_2 pmodq_1 (|t(r_1)|^2 + t(r_2)|^2) ll_varepsilon q^varepsilon \|t\|_2^2.

nodes.statement: For two different characters (or even four different characters) one may also use approximate functional equations for each L-function separately. This possibly introduces a nebentypus character chi and the error term will depend on its conductor, via the bounds for R_2 in Theorem . This may lead to better results in these cases. In particular if, as indicated in Remark , the conductor loss is reduced or even eliminated. We do not pursue this further here.
